_doc: Evidence-based pins from 114 photos analyzed. Status: confirmed = direct visual proof; candidate = was in plan but no photo proof; downgraded = previously assumed but evidence contradicts.

trip.title: Japan — April 2026
trip.subtitle: Bryan's first time in Japan · 10 days · Tokyo + Kyoto

facts.kid: Tokyo's fanciest district — land here costs $1 million per square meter!
facts.tip: Bryan's hotel: Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji (10 nights)
facts.wow: Ginza's main street closes to traffic every Sat/Sun afternoon, becoming a 'pedestrian paradise' (hokoten) since 1970.
facts.local: Locals don't really shop here - they come for department-store basement food halls (depachika) and dinners.

extra_cards.title: First night — hotel to street
extra_cards.body: Showered, hit the streets. Tokyo is shocking. NYC vibes — tall bright buildings with old history mixed in. Little shrines tucked between high rises. Alleyways lined with tiny restaurants. Ginza is a rich, safe district. Bryan walked and got his bearings. Felt the full culture shock hit. Grabbed his first meal, cautiously watched other people eat first. Late, went back to crash. A whole day of exploring in front of him.

extra_cards.title: Working out in the dark
extra_cards.body: Up at 5 AM every day. Meditation. Coffee from the konbini. Then — gym. The problem: the gym didn't open until 6. Bryan tried on the first morning at 5:30, walked in, found it dark, and went to the front desk to complain. They informed him of the hours. The hours that were, they made very clear, posted in English. He went back at 6.

extra_cards.title: The hotel was always home base
extra_cards.body: All 10 nights, same hotel, same room. Bryan's mornings were done before anyone else was up — gym, bath, breakfast, city walk — by the time the team gathered around 9. Sometimes Doug would come down to the lobby still in his pajamas, already working on his laptop. Then the prep started: high-profile meetings, Japanese translations, nerves, edits, re-edits, last-minute changes from partners. The hotel coworking space was where the day's strategy came together before walking into any room.

pins.title: Hotel Public Bath — Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji

facts.kid: Bryan's daily ritual all trip — the hotel's Large Public Bath, B1 floor of the Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji. Fully nude, shower first, communal L-shaped tub. He went once or twice a day. End of day was the best.
facts.ritual: Shoes off at the door. Strip in the locker room. Shower thoroughly — every drop of soap and shampoo rinsed — BEFORE entering the bath. Then soak. No swimsuits, no towels in the water, no phones, no lotions.
facts.wow: Japan's public-bath tradition (sentō) traces to Buddhist temple ritual bathing in the 6th century. Communal nude bathing was — and in places still is — a daily social practice, not just hygiene.
facts.local: Hotel public-bath etiquette: if someone is already in, take the opposite end. Quiet is fine; conversation isn't expected. 20–30 minutes is a normal stay. Most Mitsui Garden hotels label their facility 'Daiyokujō' (大浴場, 'large public bath') — it's communal sentō-style, with heated municipal water rather than natural hot-spring water (which would be 'onsen').

extra_cards.title: Bryan's bath routine
extra_cards.body: L-shaped hot tub, no chlorine smell, water hot as hell. He'd shampoo and shower clean as a whistle, then slide in. First time, another guy was already in — extra awkward, but 'this is the way,' so Bryan took the opposite end. 20–30 minutes most days. Twice on heavy walking days. Once he came in to two strangers; they left right as he entered. 'No chance I'd want to chat with a coworker in there, but strangers — nothing.'

extra_cards.title: Onsen vs sentō vs daiyokujō
extra_cards.body: Three Japanese bathing words with different precise meanings, often blurred in English. Onsen (温泉): natural hot spring; water heated by the earth, mineral-rich, often outdoors. Sentō (銭湯): traditional neighborhood public bath, heated municipal water, indoor, communal — a centuries-old social institution. Daiyokujō (大浴場): 'large public bath' inside a hotel, gym, or ryokan — sentō-style amenities, sometimes piped from a real onsen. The Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji's bath is a daiyokujō: cave-like stonework, two rounded tubs, basement floor.

facts.kid: Tokyo's most famous KABUKI theater — traditional Japanese drama with elaborate costumes & makeup, in a beautiful century-old building.
facts.tip: You walked past it at 10 PM your first night — right next to your hotel
facts.wow: Full shows can run 5-6 hours; locals buy 'one-act' tickets (~Y1,000) for just 30-60 min when they don't have all day.
facts.local: The current building is the FIFTH on the same plot - earthquakes, fires, and WW2 bombing rebuilt it in 1925, 1951, and 2013.

extra_cards.title: The 5th Kabuki-za building
extra_cards.body: The current Kabuki-za opened in 2013 — and it's the FIFTH building on this site. Predecessors were destroyed by fires (1921), the Great Kantō earthquake (1923), WWII firebombing (1945), and rebuilt-then-replaced in 1950. The 2013 design by Kengo Kuma keeps the classical curved-eave façade but stacks a 29-story office tower behind it — heritage out front, modern Tokyo behind. Kabuki itself dates to 1603, when a female performer named Okuni began staging it on a riverbank in Kyoto. Single-act 'hitomakumi' tickets at the side booth let you catch 45–60 minutes for ¥1,000–2,000 without committing to the full 4–5 hour program.

extra_cards.title: He almost went
extra_cards.body: Walking past Kabuki-za during the day, there was a show running. People outside buzzing. Staff handing out flyers — a traditional touring performance, not the resident company. Bryan grabbed two flyers. Stood there for a beat. The impulse was real. But Kyoto was already pulling. The flyers came home in his bag.

pins.title: Hokuto Sukiyaki — The Raw Egg Restaurant

facts.kid: A tiny solo lunch Bryan walked into off the street — individual table stoves, a mystery menu, and a dipping sauce that turned out to be raw egg. It's Hokuto, a Kyoto sukiyaki house whose first Tokyo branch had opened two days earlier.
facts.tip: Around 3 PM, Apr 19, starving after a long walk, just past Kabuki-za. The Ginza Corridor — the covered dining street under the rail tracks. Yamashita Building 2F, 6-2 Ginza, Chuo-ku.
facts.wow: Raw egg as a dipping sauce (sukiyaki-style) has been common in Japan since the Meiji era. The egg tempers the heat and adds richness — a texture most Westerners need a beat to accept.
facts.local: Sukiyaki is cooked at the table in a shallow iron pan — wagyu seared first in warishita (soy, sugar, mirin), then tofu, noodles, vegetables. Crack a raw egg into a bowl, beat it lightly, and dip each piece as you pull it from the pan.

extra_cards.title: Two days after opening
extra_cards.body: The place was Hokuto — a Kyoto sukiyaki institution. Its first Tokyo location had opened on April 17, the day Bryan landed; he walked in on the 19th, two days later, with no idea any of that was true. He just knew it looked good, and he was starving.

extra_cards.title: Starving and walking
extra_cards.body:
Bryan had been walking for hours. Hadn't eaten since morning. It was around 3 PM.

He'd just passed the Kabuki-za — people buzzing outside, flyers for a new traditional touring show, everyone excited in a way that made him wish he could stay longer. He stopped, took pictures, grabbed two of the flyers. Then hunger won.

He walked into a small restaurant that looked good — whatever that means when you're starving and can't read the menu. He was the only one inside. Individual little stoves at each table. He picked a seat and figured he'd give it a go.

extra_cards.title: You don't have to, but this is how
extra_cards.body:
The waitress was cool. Good energy, limited English, happy to talk. She found him a popular dish and brought everything out with a printed instruction sheet.

Then there was a raw egg, still in its shell.

He asked. She explained in careful broken English: after cooking the meat, Japanese people dip the meat or vegetable into the raw egg like a dipping sauce. Then she said: 'You don't have to do it if you don't want to.'

He told her: I'm in Japan. Let's give it a go.

He had mental blockers. It was delicious.

extra_cards.title: She ran after him
extra_cards.body:
He paid, told her the food was great. They laughed. He walked out and started down the block toward the hotel.

He heard someone yelling behind him.

The waitress. Running out of the restaurant, carrying the two Kabuki-za flyers — they'd fallen out of his bag into the storage basket under the seat. She ran out to make sure he didn't lose them.

Another Japanese person who looked out for him. The trip was full of them.

pins.title: Chirori the Therapy Dog — Tsukijigawa Ginza Park

facts.kid: A bronze statue honoring Chirori — Japan's very first certified therapy dog. Found abandoned with five puppies, she went on to become a national hero.
facts.tip: One minute from Higashi-Ginza station, right next to Kabuki-za. Bryan walked past this park almost every day of the trip.
facts.wow: Chirori's story directly changed Japanese law — her work with disabled and elderly patients led to a revision of Japan's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.
facts.local: The park sits on the filled-in bed of the Tsukijigawa river, which ran through Edo-era Tokyo until the Meiji era. A park named for water where there's no longer any water.

extra_cards.title: The dog who almost didn't make it
extra_cards.body: Chirori was found abandoned with five puppies, all of them days from euthanasia. A handler saw something in her and pulled her from the list. She went on to become Japan's first certified therapy dog — visiting hospitals, elderly care facilities, and homes for disabled children across the country. Her story made national news and helped lawmakers understand that animals could offer healing that medicine alone couldn't. A bronze statue was erected in 2007, one year after her death. Bryan has a rescue dog of his own. That part wasn't lost on him.

extra_cards.title: A minute with the plaque
extra_cards.body:
Bryan walked past Tsukijigawa Ginza Park almost every day of the trip — it was on the route between his hotel and the theatre. He was taking pictures of everything. He stopped, took a picture, and paused to read the plaque.

Two things landed: an abandoned dog who nearly didn't make it, and the disabled children and elderly people she went on to help. He stood there for a minute. Something about the gap between where she started and what she became.

extra_cards.title: Calling the Moon
extra_cards.body: At the edge of the park stands a second sculpture: 月を呼ぶ — 'Calling the Moon,' by sculptor 佛子泰夫. A tall figure stretching upward, arms reaching toward something just beyond reach. The park holds both in the same breath: a dog who healed people at ground level, and a figure straining toward the sky. Bryan didn't photograph it. But he walked past it.

facts.kid: A giant red-brick station that's 100+ years old. Where Bryan's shinkansen to Kyoto and back arrived/departed.
facts.tip: Departed Apr 25 morning + Arrived Apr 26 17:15 from Kyoto on NOZOMI 28
facts.wow: The red-brick Marunouchi facade is from 1914; it was bombed in WW2 and only fully restored to original spec in 2012.
facts.local: Locals never just say 'Tokyo Station' - they specify 'Yaesu side' (east) or 'Marunouchi side' (west). The two sides feel like different cities.

videos.title: Tokyo Station — arriving on the platform · 17:11

facts.kid: Tokyo's Wall Street — giant office buildings + MUJI mega-store + Imperial Palace next door.
facts.tip: You walked here Apr 22 4:53 PM after the MoD meeting
facts.wow: About 90% of land here is owned by ONE landlord: Mitsubishi Estate, since 1894 - reportedly the highest-value real estate block on Earth.
facts.local: This is salaryman lunch country. The 2nd-basement food courts in every office tower hide the best ramen and donburi shops.

extra_cards.title: Mitsubishi's London Town
extra_cards.body: Marunouchi was an empty parade ground in 1890 when the Meiji government sold the whole district to Mitsubishi for ¥1.5M (equivalent to about $1M USD at the time — a famously cheap deal in retrospect). Mitsubishi's founder asked British architect Josiah Conder to design the new district to look like London — the result was 'Ichigokan,' a red-brick boulevard nicknamed 'London Town' that defined Japanese business architecture for decades. The original Ichigokan was demolished in 1968 and faithfully reconstructed in 2009; you can visit the museum. Marunouchi today is the most concentrated Japanese-corporate-HQ district in the country.

facts.kid: The quiet, paid inner garden tucked inside the Meiji Jingu grounds — winding paths, an iris field, and a still pond with water lilies.
facts.tip: Apr 19 afternoon. Bryan kept walking deeper into the Meiji Jingu grounds and ended up here, then sat a while at the Forest Terrace cafe.
facts.wow: The Inner Garden (Gyoen) was laid out in the Meiji era at Empress Shoken's request — she loved irises. Its iris field blooms every late April and May, exactly when Bryan was there.
facts.local: Most visitors rush past the Gyoen entrance to reach the main shrine. The small admission fee keeps it quiet — the iris beds and the lily pond are the reward.

extra_cards.title: A daimyo garden by the sea
extra_cards.body: Hamarikyu was originally a private villa garden for the Tokugawa family, built starting in 1654. Its signature feature is the tidal pond — fed directly from Tokyo Bay, the water level visibly rises and falls with the tide twice a day. The teahouse (Nakajima no Ochaya) sits on stilts in the middle of the pond; you can sit on tatami, drink matcha, and eat a wagashi sweet for ¥850. The garden is bordered by Shiodome's glass office towers on one side and the bay on the other — one of the cleanest 'old Tokyo / new Tokyo' framings in the city.

facts.kid: Used to be the BIGGEST fish market in the world. Sushi for breakfast!
facts.tip: You walked here at 5:52 AM Apr 19 BEFORE it opened — sunrise market walk
facts.wow: The famous tuna auction moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the OUTER market stayed - and it's busier than ever.
facts.local: Tsukiji shop owners arrive at 3-4 AM. If you want the best stuff, be there by 8 - by 10 the tourists have it.

extra_cards.title: Tsukiji split in two
extra_cards.body: What most people call 'Tsukiji Market' today is actually just the OUTER market. The famous inner wholesale fish auction — where the giant tuna sold for record millions — moved to a new facility in Toyosu in October 2018, ending an 83-year run. The outer market (where locals and tourists buy retail fish, eat sushi breakfast, and shop for knives) stayed at the original Tsukiji site. Toyosu is more sterile and harder to access casually; Tsukiji outer is still the alive, walkable, eat-as-you-go food market.

extra_cards.title: Bryan came back on the last morning
extra_cards.body: The market visited Apr 19 for the sunrise walk. He came back Apr 27 — last morning in Japan, rain, no umbrella, Senso-ji postponed. He ended up at a nearby intersection in the rain and had a moment with a stranger. That story is on its own pin: The Umbrella Lady.

extra_cards.title: Team lunch before the meeting
extra_cards.body: Apr 24, midday. Bryan, Doug, Alex and Clair walked into the old fish market for a team lunch before an afternoon meeting. They ended up with rice bowls — the kind with a raw egg cracked on top. Good food, good crew, an easy hour before walking into a hard room. One of the trip's better team meals.

extra_cards.title: Check your behavior
extra_cards.body: Bryan kept photographing the etiquette signage all over Japan — the polite, illustrated 'please don't do this' notices aimed at tourists. In the taxi to lunch, another one: a 'STOP! Harassment' card on the seatback, six little panels covering everything from loud voices to unauthorized recording. Not scolding — just clear. He collected these the way other people collect magnets.

pins.title: The Umbrella Lady — Last Morning in Tokyo

facts.kid: Bryan's last morning in Japan. 4 AM. Pouring rain. No umbrella. A tiny old Japanese woman tried to share hers with his very tall head.
facts.tip: No photos — it was 4 AM in the rain. The shrine Bryan was going to visit didn't happen. This moment was better.
facts.wow: In Japan, umbrellas are standard all-weather gear — carried for sun as much as rain. Sunglasses are culturally associated with gangs; umbrellas are the polite default. Bryan was the only person in Tokyo without one.
facts.local: The intersection is next to the old Tsukiji fish market site. At 4 AM it's quiet except for market workers heading in early. The crowd at the light was a mix of salarymen and vendors.

extra_cards.title: The sunrise walk that didn't happen
extra_cards.body:
It was his last morning in Japan. He'd gotten no sleep. Woke up around 4 AM, wide awake, wanting to mark it properly.

The plan: subway over early, walk one of the big nearby shrines in the morning glow. Sunrise in a quiet Shinto shrine. A proper send-off.

When he woke up, it was pouring rain. He could not see the sky. He debated walking anyway. He decided it would be a waste — you couldn't see anything through the rain. So he went outside anyway, figuring he would explore the city one last time.

extra_cards.title: The only man in Tokyo without an umbrella
extra_cards.body:
He was literally the only person in Tokyo without one.

Everyone carries umbrellas here. For rain, yes — but also for sun. Sunglasses are associated with gangs; an umbrella is the polite default. Bryan, already the tallest man alive on any given Tokyo street, was now also a dripping 6-foot-something anomaly at 4 AM in a downpour.

He got more stares in those few blocks than any other moment of the trip. He decided he'd buy one just to keep the eyes off him.

extra_cards.title: She tried
extra_cards.body:
Before he could get to a store, he was at a busy intersection next to the old fish market. Waiting with everyone else for the light.

He felt something on the back of his head. He swatted it away — thought it was a bird.

It was a tiny old Japanese woman, reaching up as high as she could to hold her umbrella over his head.

He thanked her. Tried to show her he was sorry for swatting — I thought it was a bird. He doesn't know if that came across. She held the umbrella over both of them until the light changed.

When they started walking, she tried to keep holding it. She couldn't walk and hold it that high. She shook her head at him in apology and walked off.

He said arigato. He nodded. Better than a sunrise hike was a beautiful moment with a Japanese woman who tried to keep the tall ogre dry in the rain.

facts.kid: Tokyo's OLDEST temple — built in 645 AD! Bryan visited TWICE: Apr 19 daylight & Apr 27 sunrise. The whole trip was bookended by Senso-ji.
facts.history: Founded when two fisherman brothers pulled a tiny golden statue of Kannon from the Sumida River.
facts.ritual: Wave incense smoke over yourself before entering for good health.
facts.symbol: 1,500-lb red lantern at Kaminarimon Gate ('Thunder Gate').
facts.wow: A typhoon ripped the giant Kaminarimon lantern in half in 2014. The temple replaces it every ~10 years and ceremonially burns the old one.
facts.local: Skip the main path. Cut one block west to Denpoin-dori to see what Asakusa looked like a century ago.

extra_cards.title: Bryan's first shrine ritual
extra_cards.body: Threw in 100 yen (about 68 cents — the standard temple coin). One bow to acknowledge where you are. Two claps to wake the spirits — 'hello, I'm here.' Prayer — gratitude, never asking for anything specific. One more bow on the way out. Felt like an Episcopal service stripped of the teachings — tradition, faith, action, with no one trying to convert you. The ritual stayed the same all trip; the prayers and the feeling shifted from shrine to shrine.

extra_cards.title: THE LEAST FORTUNATE — Bryan's first omikuji
extra_cards.body: Cylinder maybe a foot long, packed with numbered wooden rods. Drop a coin, shake, pull one rod. Number on the rod points to a metal drawer on the wall — yours is the slip inside. Drew #31. Pulled the slip. THE LEAST FORTUNATE. The lowest fortune in the box. The whole 'your time hasn't come, you won't get what you want, be patient' rebuke. First instinct: tie it to the post and walk away — bad omikuji are bundled and burned at day's end. Second instinct, after a beat: this is the most on-the-nose, perfectly absurd first-fortune anyone in Japan could possibly draw. Kept it. Still his favorite of the trip.

extra_cards.title: Buddhist, not Shinto — the difference Bryan was riding
extra_cards.body: Senso-ji is a BUDDHIST temple (Pure Land sect), even though Bryan's ritual — coin, bow, two claps, prayer, bow — borrowed Shinto shrine etiquette. In practice most Japanese visitors blend the two: clap-style prayer at Shinto shrines (jinja), palms-pressed-together at Buddhist temples (otera). Bryan's prayer-by-instinct lined up just fine.

extra_cards.title: Omikuji — the fortune-paper system
extra_cards.body: The cylinder-and-rod fortune is called 'omikuji' (御御籤). Donate a coin, shake the cylinder, draw one numbered wooden stick, retrieve the matching paper from the numbered drawer. Senso-ji is famous for an unusually harsh distribution — about 30% of slips are 'kyō' (bad luck) or 'dai-kyō' (great bad luck), versus most temples that bias kinder. Bad fortunes get tied to a nearby rack of wire or pine — the temple bundles and ritually burns them. Bryan's THE LEAST FORTUNATE wasn't random odds; he picked one of the toughest omikuji boxes in Japan to start with.

extra_cards.title: The last morning — the plan and what actually happened
extra_cards.body: Apr 27. Last full morning in Japan. The plan was sunrise at Senso-ji — the kind of quiet you only get before the tourists arrive. Set the alarm. Checked the weather. Rain. Not drizzle — real rain. Bryan had no umbrella. He went out anyway, walked toward Tsukiji, and stood at an intersection in the rain with nowhere to be. That moment became its own thing. He made it to Senso-ji later that morning, around 8:45, temple already filling up. The sunrise visit that would have bookended the trip perfectly didn't happen. What happened instead was better.

facts.kid: Old shopping street with snacks, fans, toys. 250+ years old, ~90 little shops.
facts.food: Try ningyo-yaki (doll-shaped cake), age-manju, senbei rice crackers.
facts.wow: Many of the 250+ shops have hereditary licenses - same families running them for 6+ generations.
facts.local: Last shop on the right before the gate (Funawa) does the best age-manju in Tokyo, fried while you wait.

facts.kid: A hidden Edo-era side street near Senso-ji that most tourists skip. You found it Apr 19 11:31 — kanji photo confirmed (ä¼æ³•é™¢é€š)
facts.wow: Zero chain stores - strict preservation rules keep the whole street Edo-period in appearance.
facts.local: The maneki-neko cat figurines on the rooftops aren't decoration - they're inviting business luck for each shop below.

facts.kid: Tokyo's iconic river that runs through Asakusa — the river the Senso-ji statue legend started in!
facts.tip: Walked here right after Senso-ji at 11:39 AM Apr 19
facts.wow: Until 1888, sumo wrestlers actually fought on barges floating on this river.
facts.local: From May the Suijo Bus runs Asakusa to Hamarikyu - same route Bryan walked, seen from the water.

facts.kid: An ancient Buddhist temple right next to TOKYO TOWER. The view of the temple's curved black roof with the red-and-white Tokyo Tower behind is one of Tokyo's most iconic photos.
facts.history: Founded 1393. Family temple of the Tokugawa shoguns. Six shoguns are buried here.
facts.symbol: Hundreds of small Jizo statues with red bibs and pinwheels — memorials for unborn or deceased children
facts.ritual: Pray for safe passage of children and family
facts.wow: Tokyo Tower is 13m TALLER than the Eiffel Tower (333m vs 320m) and was built in 1958 specifically to top it.
facts.local: The little Jizo statues with red bibs are memorials for unborn children. Parents change the bibs themselves, year after year.

extra_cards.title: The Kuro-honzon — Ieyasu's blackened Amida
extra_cards.body: Zojoji's most venerated object: the Kuro-honzon (黒本尊, 'Black Principal Image'), a ~1-meter Amida Buddha statue said to have been carved in the 11th century by the Tendai monk Eshin Sōzu Genshin. Tokugawa Ieyasu adopted it as his personal protective Buddha and reportedly carried it on his major military campaigns. It is credited with granting him victory — the kanji 勝運 (shōun / 'victory luck') is associated with it. Centuries of incense smoke and prayer blackened the statue, hence its name. It's displayed publicly only three times a year (January 15, May 15, September 15).

extra_cards.title: 勝運 — the victory-luck talisman Bryan brought home
extra_cards.body: Tucked into the scrapbook: a Zojoji talisman card with an eagle illustration and two kanji — 勝運 (victory luck) at top, 成就 (fulfillment / achievement) at bottom. These are Kuro-honzon themed talismans. Bryan also kept the Daihonzan Zojo-ji ofuda wrapper, a Tokugawa mitsuba-aoi (three-leaf hollyhock) crest insert, and the printed Kuro-honzon origin pamphlet. A real Tokugawa-temple artifact set, not generic merch.

facts.kid: A small Shinto shrine tucked on the Zojoji grounds — a torii, a water basin, a stone stele. Bryan walked it without knowing it was a crow shrine.
facts.wow: The Kumano messenger is the Yatagarasu — a three-legged crow that, in legend, guided a lost emperor through the mountains. A guide-crow, on the same trip Bryan kept praying for his steps to be guided.
facts.local: Crows in Japanese culture are messengers and wise truth-tellers. The three-legged crow fits a culture where trust is built slowly, community is supportive, and wisdom passes down the generations.

extra_cards.title: The crow shrine on the grounds
extra_cards.body: Bryan walked it without knowing what it was: a small Shinto shrine tucked on the Zojoji grounds — torii, chōzuya water basin, a stone stele. It's a Kumano shrine, and the Kumano messenger is the Yatagarasu, the three-legged crow that guided a lost emperor through the mountains. He didn't learn until later that he'd stood at a crow shrine — on the same trip he kept praying for his steps to be guided.

extra_cards.title: Why Bryan loves crows
extra_cards.body:
In high school, Bryan was assigned Edgar Allan Poe — the first 'adult' writer he fell in love with. Dark and insightful. He read it the way he read everything: last minute. 11:30 PM, the house quiet, the story climaxing on a haunted house — and the grandfather clock rang. He jumped through the ceiling.

Crows fit the same pull. Intimidating, scary-looking — and the more he learned, the more fascinated he got. They solve puzzles. They use tools. They recognize human faces — there are accounts of crows escorting a girl to her school bus and throwing stones at the kids who bothered her. Protective, loyal. They bring gifts — shiny things, left for people they like. Befriending a crow is on Bryan's bucket list. He's tried: nuts and fruit left out when crows are near. It takes time to build their trust. He hasn't yet. But he will.

extra_cards.title: Crows as messengers
extra_cards.body: Bryan loves crows in folklore. Like most folklore, it takes a real characteristic and exaggerates it — and he likes that, because it's how he communicates: truth through exaggeration. It's why legends and myths land harder for him — you get a bigger meaning folded in with the exaggerated truth. Crows as messengers. Wise truth-tellers. Japan has the three-legged crow. A culture where trust takes time, where community is supportive, where wisdom passes down generations. The crow seems exactly right here.

extra_cards.title: Beware of Crows
extra_cards.body: Down the street from the shrine, a cafe (Le Pain Quotidien) had set out a hand-laminated sign — カラス注意 / 'Beware of Crows' — next to a plastic owl decoy guarding the outdoor tables. Bryan kept the photo. A crow shrine on one end of the block, a 'beware of crows' sign on the other. The same bird, held two ways: messenger and nuisance, sacred and ordinary. It seemed exactly appropriate.

pins.title: Sentai Kosodate Jizo — the Children's Shrine

facts.kid: Rows and rows of small stone statues on the Zojoji grounds — each one a memorial for a child, often dressed by the family in a knit hat and a red bib.
facts.wow: Jizo is the Buddhist guardian of children and travelers. The Sentai Kosodate Jizo at Zojoji are tended by parents, who change the little hats and bibs year after year.
facts.local: The fabric and the small additions look simple but carry everything — like a lot of things in Japan: simple and effective.

extra_cards.title: Rows of little statues
extra_cards.body: It's breathtaking before you even read about it. Rows of little statues, all looking the same — like the fox shrines, a dedicated theme repeated, all similar with minor differences. Sometimes the only difference is the fabric a family has put on a statue to give it a personality. The fabric, the small additions — so simple, and they carry so much. Bryan found himself getting lost in the similarity, then drawn into the details. Who put this hat on? Why this color? Why this pattern? A personal choice, or a cultural one?

extra_cards.title: A prayer for each family
extra_cards.body: There are two powerful but different feelings — seeing a graveyard versus seeing a single grave. Bryan tried to pause and reflect here, the way he did at every shrine. His biggest takeaway was the personal pain tied to each individual statue. He paused, and said a prayer for each of the families represented. There's a video of this one — it's that kind of place.

facts.kid: The ordinary streets between the station and Zojoji Temple — quiet sidewalks, low buildings, a city going about its morning.
facts.wow: Minato ward holds both the oldest and the newest Tokyo: Edo-era temple grounds like Zojoji sit a block from glass corporate towers and embassies.
facts.local: Tokyo's residential side streets are nearly silent even mid-morning — no honking, no street noise, just footsteps and bicycle bells.
facts.tip: Photographed around 10:25 on Day 7, on the approach to Zojoji.

facts.kid: A huge forest shrine with 100,000 trees in Tokyo!
facts.deity: Spirits of Emperor Meiji and Empress ShÅken
facts.wow: The 100,000-tree forest was donated from every prefecture in 1920 - it's a fake 'old forest,' only a century old.
facts.local: Saturday mornings you'll often see a full white-kimono wedding procession crossing the main path - locals plan around it.

extra_cards.title: Second omikuji — 'from the empress'
extra_cards.body: Bryan drew a second fortune at Meiji Jingu — and this one wasn't a tier-graded slip at all. The shrine uses a waka mikuji system: instead of 'good' or 'bad' luck, you draw one of 30 specific poems by Emperor Meiji or Empress Shōken, and the poem is the guidance. Bryan drew #22, a poem by Empress Shōken on purity of heart. 'From the empress' was literal — see the dedicated card below for the full poem. He called it 'a cool one too.' But the Senso-ji THE LEAST FORTUNATE stays his favorite — you can't beat the on-the-nose perfection of drawing the worst fortune in the box on your first try in Japan.

extra_cards.title: The waka mikuji — Empress Shōken's poem #22
extra_cards.body:
Meiji Jingu's fortune system is unique. Most omikuji rank you on a tier (great-good → great-bad). Meiji Jingu's instead is a waka mikuji: one of 30 specific poems composed by Emperor Meiji or Empress Shōken, drawn at random — the poem itself is the guidance. No good or bad. Bryan drew #22, an Empress Shōken poem on purity of heart:

朝ごとに  むかふ鏡の  くもりなく  あらまほしきは  心なりけり

Asagotoni / Mukau kagami no / Kumori naku / Aramahoshiki wa / Kokoro narikeri

'Every morning / we gaze into our mirrors / which are unblemished; / oh, that we could attain / such a purity of soul.'

Empress Shōken wrote ~30,000 waka in her lifetime. This is one of her most-cited.

extra_cards.title: The Inner Garden — iris beds and forest paths
extra_cards.body:
After the main shrine, Bryan kept walking deeper into the grounds. The Meiji Jingu Inner Garden (明治神宮内苑) is a separate area — bamboo-roped gravel paths, old-growth forest, an iris garden that blooms every late April and May. The garden was built in the Meiji era at the Empress's request; she loved irises.

At 14:59 he was still there. The Forest Terrace café inside the grounds: cold coffee, chocolate cake, Evian. He kept the receipt. He sat for a while.

Meiji Jingu is the kind of place that takes longer than you plan for.

facts.kid: Japan's Ministry of Defense — like the Pentagon. Bryan met with teams there twice during the trip's government engagements (Apr 22 and Apr 24).
facts.tip: Visited twice — Apr 22 PM and Apr 24 PM. Visitor badge + martial arts poster confirmed inside.
facts.wow: The MoD sits on the site of the old Imperial Army HQ - where Tojo (the WW2 PM) had his office.
facts.local: The Ichigaya Memorial Hall on the grounds is where Mishima Yukio committed seppuku in 1970. Open by reservation only.

extra_cards.title: What Bryan brought back from MoD HQ
extra_cards.body:
From the visit Bryan came home with a small set of genuine Japan-MoD artifacts in his Kichi-in-chō ('Base Stamp Book' — a JSDF-themed collector's book with an F-2 jet on the navy cover):

• 防衛省来省記念 visit-commemoration stamp — Reiwa 8 fiscal year, with the paulownia government crest, the 任務遂行 ('Mission accomplished') seal, a Japan-flag stamp, and a serial-number stamp.
• An embroidered MoD HQ patch (Ministry of Defense · Tokyo Japan) depicting the Ichigaya A-Building tower with antennas — the building Bryan met inside.
• An embroidered Rising Sun flag (旭日旗 / Kyokujitsu-ki) patch — Japan's naval ensign.

These are uncommon items for a foreign visitor and a quiet badge of how seriously the visit was received.

facts.kid: Your first dinner in Japan — a tablet-order Tokyo izakaya. You had Iyoshi Cola (Japan's craft cola).
facts.tip: Apr 18 9:50 PM. Sober: cola + water.
facts.wow: Iyoshi Cola was invented in 2018 by a fourth-generation Chinese-herb pharmacist - it's a literal craft cola from Tokyo.
facts.local: Tablet-order izakaya only became normal post-2020. Older locals still find them rude.

extra_cards.title: Izakaya etiquette — the otoshi 'gift'
extra_cards.body: Sit down at an izakaya and a small appetizer arrives unrequested — pickled vegetables, simmered tofu, a tiny salad. This is 'otoshi' (お通し), and it is NOT free. It's a soft cover charge in food form, usually ¥300–¥500 per person, that signals you're an actual customer not just stopping to use the bathroom. Refusing it is technically allowed but socially awkward and often won't save you the charge.

facts.kid: A pub-style restaurant in Akihabara where Bryan had jasmine tea while co-workers had drinks.
facts.tip: Receipt confirmed Apr 21 9:32 PM. Total ¥8,514 (cash). Phone 03-58254520. Table C1.
facts.wow: 'Izakaya' literally means 'stay-sake-shop' - originally sake shops that let you drink on-site instead of buying to go.
facts.local: The 'free' otoshi appetizer that appears is NOT free - it's the table charge in food form, Y300-500/person.

extra_cards.title: Make it an 18 oz
extra_cards.body: After the big day — JNI partner meeting, the Ministry of Defense — the team hit IBREW to decompress. Everyone ordered a beer. The waitress went around: 12 or 18 oz? Bryan was dying of thirst. When his turn came: 'Green tea... make it an 18 oz.' The table understood immediately. Best non-drinking work joke of the trip.

extra_cards.title: The license
extra_cards.body:
Bryan showed the team his drivers license — a heavier photo from a few years back, just an awful picture. He showed Clair first. She literally fell off her chair laughing. It got passed around the table. Bryan leaned into every second of it.

A few nights later at the NSSOL partner dinner, he ran it back: told the table 'Clair said this photo is awful of me, so rude and not true' — handed it around. Everyone agreed with Clair. Solid go-to joke. Two different crowds, same result.

facts.kid: A traditional Japanese grilled-chicken-skewer place. Bryan saw exotic cuts on the menu — quail eggs, knee cartilage, the bit between heart and liver!
facts.tip: Apr 22 8:07 PM. After the rainy Tokyo nightlife wander.
facts.wow: Real yakitori specialists use 30+ DIFFERENT chicken parts - organs Western butchers throw away.
facts.local: Order 'omakase' (chef's choice) for the full course. Picking individual skewers off the menu marks you as a tourist.

extra_cards.title: Clair's list
extra_cards.body:
Clair had been planning her restaurants for weeks before the trip. Google Map pins, notes, ratings — she was the walking Yelp. Every evening was her pick. Some had long waits. Bryan hated just standing in line, but they talked and joked, and her places were always worth it.

This one was a specialty yakitori place she'd had circled. Organ cuts, cartilage, things that aren't on tourist menus. She knew exactly what to order.

extra_cards.title: What you actually eat at a real yakitori restaurant
extra_cards.body:
Yakitori means 'grilled chicken' — but at a place like this, that's barely the point. The menu goes deep.

Knee cartilage: chewy, almost crunchy, charred at the edges. Tsunagi: the connecting tissue between the heart and the liver — earthy, rich, nothing like a standard skewer. Momotare: thigh with house tare sauce. Quail eggs, grilled whole on skewers.

The Japanese philosophy about offcuts is the opposite of most cuisines: the unusual parts are prized, not discarded. Bryan passed on the chicken hearts — stomach's limit — but everything else went down.

extra_cards.title: After the government rooms
extra_cards.body:
The afternoon had been the first MoD meeting — the team's first real performance together. Japan's government district. Big rooms, formal interpretation, topics that mattered.

By 8 PM they were at a yakitori counter, passing skewers. Nobody needed to talk about the meeting. The food did the transition.

facts.kid: A traditional multi-course Japanese dinner — sashimi, grilled fish, tiny artistic dishes — with the NSSOL business team.
facts.tip: Apr 23 7:35-8:24 PM. Group photo at the zen-style restaurant with the NSSOL team.
facts.wow: Kaiseki has 9-13 strict courses in fixed order (appetizer to sashimi to grilled to simmered to fried to vinegared to rice to soup to dessert) - same sequence since the 1500s.
facts.local: Kaiseki etiquette: eat in the order served, don't mix courses; the chef plates each in sequence for a reason.

extra_cards.title: The dinner NSSOL wanted to give
extra_cards.body: Great meetings with the NSSOL partner team and the joint government customer. Tons of new potential business and upside. NSSOL wanted to treat the team to a proper celebration meal. Clair had been hyping this dinner all week — looking forward to it more than anyone on the team. It was everything she promised. Multiple traditional courses, all different, all delicious. Puffer fish appeared again — round two for Bryan. Also lived. Still only ok tasting.

extra_cards.title: Comfortable friends
extra_cards.body: Jokes all night. Bryan's drivers license made another lap of the table. Alex and his NSSOL research counterpart have become real friends over the course of the partnership — BFFs across 8,000 miles. They took a photo outside the restaurant standing back to back, like the album cover they deserved. The table talked business, swapped stories about their countries and cultures, laughed a lot. 'We eat dinner like comfortable friends.' That was the night in a sentence.

facts.kid: Where you had your 'best dinner ever' (your handwritten words!). Wagyu shabu-shabu — thinly sliced beef cooked in dashi broth at the table.
facts.tip: Apr 24 7:38-10:23 PM. Signed menu from the table. WAGYU BURGER doodle.
facts.wow: 'Shabu-shabu' is onomatopoeia - the SOUND of beef swishing in broth.
facts.local: Wagyu shabu at this tier runs Y15-30K/person. A signed menu makes it a milestone meal in Tokyo.

menu.name: Wagyu shabu-shabu
menu.note: Thin slices swished in dashi at the table; dipped in goma (sesame) or ponzu

extra_cards.title: Origins of shabu-shabu
extra_cards.body: Introduced in Osaka in 1952 at a restaurant called Suehiro, adapted from a Mongolian instant-boiled mutton hot pot. The name imitates the swish-swish sound of meat moving through broth.

extra_cards.title: The signed menu
extra_cards.body:
Doug's last night. He was flying out the next morning. Six people, six countries, one menu passed around the table.

Saul wrote 'best dinner ever!' Clair drew a bald-head doodle of Bryan and added 'this is the best thing EVER' in her best annoying-little-sister energy. Doug drew something that gets blurred for the kids' version. Alex wrote something in Italian — translation still pending. Vicky drew a wagyu burger.

Bryan signed his name.

The menu came home. It's in the scrapbook.

facts.kid: A wagyu beef restaurant from a 5-generation family — the meat-merchant tradition started in 1962.
facts.tip: Apr 26 10:08 PM. After Pokemon Center. Last Tokyo dinner.
facts.wow: True A5 wagyu has 35%+ intramuscular fat (vs ~6% for top USDA Prime). That marbling is why it melts at body temperature.
facts.local: Most '5-generation' meat shops are post-WW2 lineage. Japan's old wagyu trade was disrupted, then rebuilt from the 1950s onward.

extra_cards.title: The team joke
extra_cards.body:
All week, Clair had been picking the restaurants. High-end Japanese places with perfect meat and delicate fish. Nobody complained — the food was always exceptional. But one running joke in the group: someone on the team just wanted a wagyu burger.

Mentioned it multiple times a day. Didn't happen.

After everyone went their separate ways — some to the airport, some to other hotels — the group chat lit up with wagyu burger photos. Bryan was still in Tokyo. He hadn't had one either.

Tonight was the night.

extra_cards.title: An hour in line
extra_cards.body:
Google Maps. Highly rated. Sign out front promoting its rankings. And a line.

Bryan got in it. Caught up on texts, went through photos, stood there alone for about an hour. Not many parties of one.

When he finally reached the front, the host wouldn't seat him. Told him to get back in line. Bryan asked why — he was next. The host moved past him to the family of four behind him and said it would be a few minutes.

He had no idea what was happening. He was starving. It was late. He asked again, clearly: he'd been waiting in line, when would he be seated? The host said he needed to wait.

The family behind him — tourists, Middle East or South Asia — heard the whole thing. When the host came back out, they spoke up. He's been waiting. He's in front of us.

The host had thought Bryan cut the line. Once it was sorted, Bryan was seated.

extra_cards.title: The menu, the story, the flame
extra_cards.body:
The menu told the story before the food arrived. The history of the cows. The specific breed, what makes wagyu different — the fat marbling, the grading, the way the cattle are raised. The owner's search for the right source.

This is what people rave about Japanese food. The level of care. Making the best possible version of the thing, not just the thing. A burger is a burger. A wagyu burger at a place like this is the result of someone's life's work.

They brought it out and put a flame to it. The fat crisped at the edge. Bryan was starving. He's also pretty sure it was the best burger he's ever had.

He called Kel. Got some sleep. One last morning in Tokyo, then the long flight home.

facts.kid: A traditional fried-pork-cutlet lunch with shredded cabbage. Your first meal with the team.
facts.tip: Apr 20 12:54 PM. 4 people: Bryan + 3 colleagues.
facts.wow: Tonkatsu was invented in 1899 in Tokyo as a Western adaptation. 'Katsu' comes from the English word 'cutlet.'
facts.local: The shredded raw cabbage isn't garnish - it's served first, intentionally, to help digest the heavy pork. Pile it on; eat it first.

extra_cards.title: Tonkatsu — the Western dish that became Japanese
extra_cards.body: Tonkatsu was invented in 1899 at a Western-style restaurant in Tokyo's Ginza. The original called it 'pork cutlet' (cutlet → 'katsu'), borrowed from French cotelette. Within a generation it was eaten with chopsticks over rice, dipped in tonkatsu sauce, and served with shredded raw cabbage on the side. Now it's read as quintessentially Japanese. Bryan's first team meal landed on one of the most successful immigrant dishes in Japan's food history.

facts.kid: 🎮 A WHOLE STORE of nothing but Pokemon stuff — cards, plushies, T-shirts, even snacks!
facts.tip: Apr 26, ~8:35-8:46 PM. 38 items, ¥48,083 total. Charizard coin purse + cards in the haul.
facts.wow: The Pokemon Company is a JOINT venture between Nintendo, Game Freak, and Creatures Inc. - not Nintendo alone, which surprises most fans.
facts.local: Each Pokemon Center sells city-exclusive Pikachu plushies in local outfits - Tokyo Tower outfit, Kyoto kimono, etc. Collector bait.

extra_cards.title: The plushie haul came home
extra_cards.body: Bryan came home with a Pokemon Center bag stuffed with plushies — a small zoo of them. On the night back in Virginia, he and Kelly spread the whole haul out on the couch with the tags still on. Some were set aside for kids and family, some kept for the house. One Pikachu was claimed for a shelf in their home — the one that made it through the sorting and stays.

facts.kid: A modern café with free WiFi where Bryan worked on his MacBook before the MoD meeting.
facts.tip: Apr 22 9:22 AM. Cushioned seating, plants.
facts.wow: Tokyo has 600+ dedicated coworking spaces - more than NYC - but most locals just work at chain cafes (Doutor, Komeda).
facts.local: Cafe-as-office etiquette: order something every 90 min, or get politely asked to leave.

facts.kid: Bryan's daily breakfast spot — the Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji's top-floor restaurant on the 14th floor. Cool city view, opens at 7. He was usually first in.
facts.tip: Hotel-issued gold coin tokens at check-in redeem for free coffee or beer at the lobby bar near the entrance — Mitsui Garden Hotel signature perk.
facts.wow: After two days of Japanese breakfasts (fish, salmon roe, miso) Bryan switched to greek yogurt + fruit + eggs + bread. Every other meal of the day was Japanese-heavy — fiber and lightness for breakfast made the rest of the day work.
facts.local: The hipster-looking egg + grain bowl most foreign guests photograph from this restaurant is actually a hybrid: Japanese ingredients (pickled veg, herbs, pink radish) on a Western base. Common in Tokyo hotel restaurants targeting overseas guests.

extra_cards.title: Bryan's morning routine — anchored here
extra_cards.body: 5 AM wake-up, 10-minute meditation, walk to a 7-Eleven/Lawson/Family Mart for a rice triangle and coffee, gym at 6, public bath after, breakfast at 7 — first in, gold coin pocketed. After Day 2 he dropped Japanese breakfasts (salmon roe is intense at 7 AM) and ran greek yogurt + fruit + eggs + bread instead. This was the anchor.

facts.kid: A futuristic metal-and-glass mega-station that looks like a spaceship — surprising in old Kyoto!
facts.tip: Arrived from Tokyo Sat AM, departed back on NOZOMI 28 (15:01 Sun)
facts.wow: Hiroshi Hara's 1997 design hides a 15-story 'Sky Garden' on the roof - a free public observation deck most tourists miss.
facts.local: From the rooftop terrace you can see Higashi-Honganji, the Toji pagoda, AND the mountains Bryan hiked. Best free view in Kyoto.
