facts.kid: 10,000 bright orange torii gates climbing a mountain! Each donated by a family or business. Bryan climbed Mt. Inari solo — a four-hour off-trail wander to the summit and back.
facts.history: Founded 711 AD. Head shrine of 30,000 Inari shrines across Japan.
facts.deity: Inari ÅŒkami — Shinto god/goddess of rice, foxes, and prosperity
facts.ritual: Foxes (kitsune) are Inari's messengers — fox statues hold keys or scrolls.
facts.symbol: Endless tunnel of vermilion torii gates.
facts.wow: The '10,000 torii' is folk talk - real count is closer to 32,000 including miniatures, each paid for by an individual or business praying for prosperity.
facts.local: Skip the famous Senbon Torii crowd-tunnel. The back trails above the Yotsutsuji intersection are nearly empty even at midday - exactly where Bryan went.

extra_cards.title: The main shrine and the start of the torii
extra_cards.body: Bryan came off the bullet train with no plan and no hotel, walked up through the shop-lined streets, and arrived at the main hall of Fushimi Inari — the head shrine of some 30,000 Inari shrines across Japan. He did his ritual — coin, bow, two claps, prayer, bow — then stepped into the Senbon Torii, the famous tunnel of thousands of vermilion gates, each one donated and inscribed. The gate corridor is where most visitors stop. Bryan kept going — four hours, off-trail, all the way to the summit and back.

extra_cards.title: Why foxes at Inari shrines
extra_cards.body: The fox (kitsune) is the messenger of Inari Ōkami, the Shinto kami of rice, business, and prosperity. Fox statues at Inari shrines often hold a key (to the rice granary) or a scroll (the prayer of the petitioner). Fushimi Inari Taisha is the head shrine of an Inari network of ~30,000 sub-shrines across Japan — which is why fox statues show up at small neighborhood shrines all over the country.

facts.kid: The packed, shop-lined street that leads up to the shrine gates — food stalls, fox-shaped everything, and a coffee stop before the climb.
facts.tip: Bryan came straight off the bullet train with a bare-bones backpack, no hotel booked, no plan past 'go to Fushimi.'
facts.local: The approach is cash-country. Bryan kept hitting cash-only counters and regretting not carrying a coin wallet — a running theme of the whole trip.

extra_cards.title: Coffee, an egg sandwich, and no coins
extra_cards.body: Off the train, into the crowd, up the shop-lined approach. Bryan stopped for a coffee and an egg sandwich before the climb — and hit the cash-only wall again. Everywhere on this street wanted coins, and he never did get a coin wallet. He ate, shouldered the little backpack, and turned for the gates.

pins.title: Fushimi Inari — bamboo & the Merc shrines

facts.kid: Past the Yotsutsuji crossroads the crowds thin out — bamboo, quiet trail, and dozens of little fox-statue sub-shrines climbing the mountain.
facts.tip: Bryan called these the 'Merc shrines' — the stone foxes all looked like Mercury, his dog.
facts.local: Above the Senbon Torii, the path branches into back trails most tourists never take. This is where the climb stops being a photo op and becomes a walk.

extra_cards.title: The bamboo and the 'guide me' meditation
extra_cards.body: The trail ran through bamboo — it reminded Bryan of the icicle room at teamLab, the one quiet beat repeating. He walked it turning the same thought over: guide my steps. The same prayer from the Buddha's-footprints stone. Carved-up bamboo he could have done without, but mostly it was green, still, and his.

extra_cards.title: Mercury in the fox statues
extra_cards.body: Bryan called the fox-statue shrines 'Merc shrines.' Not for the look of them — for Mercury, his dog. The stone kitsune at Inari shrines have a recognizable face: alert, watchful, broad-headed, slightly goofy. Bryan saw Mercury in every one. Kelly had spotted Mercury on a friend's social-media post months earlier; they acted on it and adopted him. What felt random became central.

extra_cards.title: The prayer for Mercury
extra_cards.body: At one of the fox-statue sub-shrines on the climb, Bryan stopped and did the ritual — coin, bow, two claps, prayer, bow — and the prayer was for Mercury. Gratitude that Kelly happened to see that post. Gratitude that they took action on a seemingly random thing. He got emotional. The prayer closed with a request: that he be a good and responsible owner, and that Mercury live a long, full life. One of the off-trail emotional anchors of the whole trip.

extra_cards.title: The Merc good luck charm
extra_cards.body: Among the things Bryan brought back from Fushimi Inari was a small wallet-sized metal card with the kitsune etched on it — a pocket shrine, blessed as a good-luck charm. He claimed it on the spot as his 'Merc good luck charm.' Then he and Kelly used Google Translate on it: it's only good for ONE YEAR — the only charm in the haul with an expiration date. The plan: keep it for the year of luck, then pass it to someone else for theirs. Pass-the-Merc as a rolling tradition.

pins.title: Fushimi Inari — the back road & the endless stairs

facts.kid: A back-country stretch off the main mountain — a woodshop, a quiet local shrine, a hand-written sign, and a set of stairs that went straight up.
facts.tip: Bryan's legs nearly gave out on these stairs. The vending machines along the way felt like a gift.
facts.local: There was no one on this part of the climb. The hidden cluster of shrines off the road — foxes, waterfalls behind curtains — Bryan called the best shrine visit of the whole trip.

extra_cards.title: The forgotten cluster — the best shrine visit yet
extra_cards.body: Just off the road, before the path turned up the mountain, Bryan found a cluster of shrines — so many of them, no one around. Identical little shrines side by side. Stairs that were killer. Little shrines with waterfalls behind curtains. He could walk and explore and have the moments entirely to himself. Maybe the best shrine visit of the trip.

extra_cards.title: The endless stairs
extra_cards.body: Past a woodshop where a couple was cleaning up, past a local community shrine, there was a hand-written sign with the mountain's name and then stairs — straight up, no end in sight. Bryan's legs almost fell off. Then, near the top, a line of vending machines. 'The Lord answers prayers.' He bought water and kept climbing.

facts.kid: The shrine at the top of Mt. Inari — reached after a long, tired climb. Bryan said it felt like the movies.
facts.tip: Tiny personalized torii gates cover the summit shrine — people carry their own up the mountain and leave them.
facts.local: There's a charm shop and a place to light candles at the peak. Bryan lit one at a big shrine and bought a few candles to bring home.

extra_cards.title: Felt like the movies
extra_cards.body: Bryan bowed at the gate, exhausted, and walked up. He started hearing voices. He saw the shrine — the top of the mountain shrine. It felt like the movies: the long, tired journey, and now an old man with a long beard would tell him his destiny. Turns out it was a shrine and some tourists. Still cool though.

extra_cards.title: Little asks and big prayers
extra_cards.body: All over the summit shrine were tiny personalized torii gates — people had carried them up the mountain and left them. Bryan had read up on Fushimi before going, but nowhere had he read about bringing your own gate. He'd have done it. He stood looking at other people's gates — a tourist wanting an experience, maybe someone with a sick kid trying everything — and figured it was full of little asks and big prayers, like everywhere people go looking for guidance. He made his own. Little asks and big prayers.

pins.title: Fushimi Inari — the descent & the rescue

facts.kid: Coming down the mountain, Bryan helped two lost travelers from Singapore find their way off Mt. Inari and down to the train station.
facts.tip: On the way down he realized the famous tourist gate-tunnels have normal stairs the whole way up — he'd taken the hard way without knowing.
facts.local: The descent runs through a quiet residential area at the base of the mountain — big houses, no one outside, weirdly still.

extra_cards.title: The descent epiphany
extra_cards.body: Somewhere on the way down, Bryan realized it: the famous gate tunnels — the ones tourists travel miles for — go all the way up, with normal stairs the whole way. He'd taken the insane, get-lost-on-the-mountain stairs without knowing there was an easy path. He laughed, and the obvious epiphany flooded in. Guided steps, or me wandering? The path less traveled? The journey is the actual destination. All of them, as he passed through the gorgeous gates on the walk down.

extra_cards.title: The rescue — the two Singaporean women
extra_cards.body: Down near the boulder shrines, Bryan heard two women shouting. They were from Singapore — they'd wanted adventure, picked Japan, and this mountain was way too much adventure. No signs, steep road, and they were over it. Bryan's one real skill: mountain directions. Boy Scout since forever — you either go up or you go down, find the path. He explained his reasoning; they said whatever, we'll follow you. He helped them down the steep parts, and they walked out together through a quiet residential neighborhood to the train station. Then they asked if he'd ever been to America — no, they said, they'd never go, they hear it's too dangerous. He couldn't stop thinking about that for the rest of the trip.

facts.kid: A small but historic Shinto shrine called 'Kyoto's Ise' because it's modeled after the famous Ise Grand Shrine. It has a sacred cave and a small spring.
facts.history: Founded ~5th century AD according to legend — one of the OLDEST shrines in Kyoto.
facts.deity: Amaterasu ÅŒmikami — Shinto sun goddess (and ancestor of the Imperial line)
facts.ritual: Pass through the cave shrine of Amano-Iwato to symbolically rebirth
facts.symbol: Inner shrine modeled after Ise + a sacred spring
facts.wow: 'Daijingu' means 'great divine shrine' - only Ise-affiliated shrines may use the title. Himukai got it because legend says Amaterasu rested here.
facts.local: The Amano-Iwato cave shrine reenacts the myth of the sun goddess hiding in a cave. Crawling through it = symbolic rebirth.

extra_cards.title: Meeting Max on the way up
extra_cards.body:
Bryan's solo Kyoto day was supposed to be a hike on the Higashiyama trail. The shrine at the end wasn't even certain. He started up past the crowds — they thinned fast. Beware-of-monkey signs along the way (he's got the photo). Higher up, he found two young Japanese guys resting, looking at their phones to figure out where the trail led; no reception. They asked Bryan, 'What's the goal? What's the destination?' Bryan said, 'I don't know. The trail leads up, so I'm walking up.' They laughed. He kept walking.

A few minutes later, a young guy was hiking right behind him — early 20s, Russian. **Max.** They rested together at the next fork, then again at the one after that. Bryan kept it vague about himself. Max had graduated from one of Russia's top tech universities; worked at a software company that sold to universities; used Claude for work projects. They talked about Claude a lot. Bryan said he'd love to see Russian architecture but the current situation makes that hard. Max said the same about the US. The kind of conversation you can only have when you're both far from home and tired.

The trail got rough — straight climbing, pulling up with roots, near-slips on the way down. Bryan kept his walking stick the whole time for trail support and in case of monkeys. He ran out of water. Max gave him some of his.

They reached what they thought was the peak. **Nothing was there.** No shrine. No view. Just more trees. Max was bummed: 'this is it?!' Bryan laughed and said yeah, I guess. Max admitted he didn't come to Japan just for nature — he came for temples. Some mountain runners ran past them, a marathon up the mountain. That looked crazy. They started walking down following a sign toward a shrine — figured they'd at least see something on the way.

extra_cards.title: The worshipper-only sign and the family setting the pace
extra_cards.body:
Eventually the trail brought them to a shrine — and a vending machine. Bryan was so thirsty after the climb. He bought one for himself, then one for Max for the earlier water share.

The first shrine was smaller. Bryan did his ritual — coin, bow, two claps, prayer, bow. Then walked up toward the bigger one.

There was a sign outside the bigger shrine. **Worshippers only** — or something like that. Bryan was stuck. His rule for the whole trip had been: experience as much as you can, respectfully. So what does this sign mean for that? Should he go in?

He asked Max. Max didn't know. Max said he'd chill outside — either exhausted or just tired of tagging along; both fair.

Bryan debated. He decided he'd go in respectfully — worship the way he did at every other shrine. Take pictures only if it felt OK and no one was around. He didn't want anyone seeing him and feeling disrespected. He'd respected every photo-restriction sign all trip; no sign here, but the principle held.

Inside, a family was already there — 50ish parents and a teen/20s daughter. They moved slowly. Observed each part slowly. Did each piece of the shrine slowly. The daughter trailed her parents, doing the same thing in her own slightly more personal way. Bryan made sure to match the pace. Bows, prayers, claps, yen — done the way he'd done them all trip, just at the family's tempo. He stayed a good distance away to give them their space and to have his own.

extra_cards.title: The old man, the cave, and my favorite goodbye
extra_cards.body:
After the main shrine there was a little windy path up. At the end of the path: a small cave. Outside the cave was an older Japanese man with a cane sitting on a bench. Bryan nodded and walked toward the cave entrance. The man said something loudly in broken English. Bryan thought that was it — game over, leave tourist. He walked over and said *sumimasen* (excuse me), motioned to his ear like 'I didn't hear you.' The man motioned his hand above his own head and said **'be careful of your head.'**

Bryan laughed and thanked him. He's the tallest man in this country walking into a cave. The cane-man wasn't kicking him out — he was looking out for him.

The cave (Amano-Iwato — the legendary cave where the sun goddess hid, recreated here as a symbolic-rebirth tunnel) was shaped with sharp turns so it felt properly enclosed and cave-like. Obvious Jesus-and-tomb vibes the whole way through. In the middle: a tiny shrine. Bryan said his prayer there — and the prayer was very Jesus-resurrection-tomb-themed, given where he was. He emerged from the cave a new man. Said it felt mostly the same, but — yeah baby.

**His favorite shrine of the entire trip.**

He grabbed shrine gear on the way out. One for himself. Others to gift. They had kid-fortunes — a Shinto kids'-church kind of thing — so he grabbed a bunch for family and friends' kids. Grabbed one for Max too.

Saw Max on the way out. Told him about the cave. Said, *hey bud, here's a shrine thing. No idea what it means. Hope it's cool. Fun day. Have a good life.* And dipped out.

(Saw Max one more time briefly on the way out.) Great hike. No monkeys. Great shrine. **Max is a good kid. Thanks for the water, pal.**

facts.kid: An 80+ KM official hiking trail that loops the mountains around Kyoto. You hiked the Higashiyama section — marker #37 photo proves it!
facts.tip: Apr 26 11:43 AM trail marker. Led to Himukai Daijingu.
facts.wow: The Higashiyama section links 9 World Heritage temples - including Kiyomizu, Ginkaku-ji, and Nanzen-ji.
facts.local: Marker #37 sits north of Nanzen-ji, near the Philosopher's Path. Most Kyoto tourists never know the trail exists.

extra_cards.title: Meeting Max, hiking past the peak
extra_cards.body: Bryan didn't know what was at the end of the trail. He just walked up. The crowds thinned fast. Beware-of-monkey signs along the way. Higher up he met two Japanese hikers resting — they asked his destination. He said 'I don't know — the trail leads up.' Behind them on the trail: a Russian kid in his early twenties. **Max.** They hiked together, rested together, talked about Claude (Max used it at work — software for universities), nearly slipped on the steep parts, split his water. They reached what they thought was the peak: no shrine, no view, just trees. Max — who came to Japan for temples, not nature — was bummed. They walked down toward a shrine sign, figuring they'd at least see something. What they found was Himukai Daijingu. **The full story is on that pin.**

videos.title: Morning start — heading up the Higashiyama Trail · 09:42
Upper trail — deeper into the mountain · 10:55

pins.title: Okazaki — the walk to the trailhead

facts.kid: The long morning wander from the hotel toward the mountain — a Kyoto neighborhood packed with little temples, shrines, stone monuments, and a memorial or two on nearly every block.
facts.tip: Bryan walked this whole stretch on foot, no plan past 'head for the trail.' It passes Kyoto City Zoo in Okazaki.
facts.local: Okazaki and north Higashiyama are layered with history — most of it the kind tour buses never stop for. The walk is the point.

extra_cards.title: Layered history, block by block
extra_cards.body: The walk from the Marriott toward the Kyoto Round Trail ran through Okazaki — a neighborhood where stone steles, war memorials, bronze statues, and small temple compounds sit between ordinary houses. Bryan stopped to read a real-estate listings board, wondering what it costs to live here. It's the stretch that holds Daiko-ji and its Buddha's Footprints stone. He passed Kyoto City Zoo on the way. The walk to the trailhead was its own small pilgrimage.

facts.kid: A major Zen temple with a giant red-brick aqueduct running right through the grounds — built in the 1800s, still carrying water today.
facts.tip: The Kyoto Round Trail routes straight through Nanzen-ji. Bryan reached it as a waypoint on the climb, not a destination.
facts.wow: Nanzen-ji was founded in 1291 and ranks above all other Rinzai Zen temples in Japan. The Suirokaku aqueduct that cuts through it is part of the Lake Biwa Canal, finished in 1890.
facts.local: Most visitors photograph the aqueduct arches and leave. The moss gardens and the trail behind it are quiet even at midday.

extra_cards.title: The aqueduct in the temple
extra_cards.body: Modern infrastructure threaded through an ancient Zen temple: the Suirokaku, a red-brick Roman-style aqueduct, runs right through the Nanzen-ji grounds. Bryan came up on it as a waypoint — the Kyoto Round Trail passes straight through here — moss gardens, stone lanterns, the brick arches, and then the path kept climbing into the forest.

facts.kid: Old neighborhood where you might still see GEISHA walking to work! Wooden machiya houses, lanterns, stone streets.
facts.tip: Dusk walk Sat night + Sun morning with etiquette signs
facts.wow: Real geiko (Kyoto's word for geisha) number around 80 active. Tourist photo-harassment got so bad some Gion private streets banned non-resident photography in 2024.
facts.local: The geiko you might glimpse at dusk are heading TO work, not posing. Don't follow, don't photograph, don't touch.

extra_cards.title: Geiko vs maiko
extra_cards.body: Kyoto uses different words than Tokyo: 'geiko' instead of 'geisha' (the full-fledged performer), and 'maiko' for the apprentice. A maiko trains for ~5 years before becoming a geiko, and the visual difference is the kimono and obi (maiko wear longer trailing obi 'darari' style) plus the hair (maiko hair uses elaborate ornaments — kanzashi — that change with the season). Both work primarily in invitation-only tea houses (ochaya) along Hanami-koji and Pontocho streets. Tourists almost never see them up close. The figures sometimes spotted on Hanami-koji in costume are usually rental-kimono tourists, not real geiko or maiko.

facts.kid: Kyoto's main river with stone embankments. At night, traditional restaurants light up along the banks.
facts.tip: Apr 25 7:32 PM walk along the river — your first Kyoto evening
facts.wow: In summer, restaurants extend wooden 'kawayuka' platforms over the river - Kyoto's only legal way to dine literally above moving water.
facts.local: Couples on the riverbank sit at almost exactly equal spacing (~1.8m apart) - a Kyoto urban legend that turned out to be measurably true.

extra_cards.title: The detour that took hours
extra_cards.body:
Bryan was already tired when he found it. He'd been walking across Kyoto toward his hotel — a walk that was already taking longer than expected. He'd taken videos along the way, called Kel at some point. The sun was going down.

Then he saw the river.

The hotel was close-ish. But a river.

He turned off his route and went down random alleys until he found the embankment. Couples sat together at the edge, spaced evenly, the way couples do in Kyoto. It was romantic and calm. It reminded him of Amsterdam — the light, the water, the sense that a city knows how to rest.

He sat for a while. Rested. Missed Kel.

Eventually he decided he was actually tired and headed to the hotel. He didn't mention the detour to the front desk the next morning when she asked how many hours the walk took.

extra_cards.title: Equal spacing — measurably true
extra_cards.body: The Kamogawa couple-spacing phenomenon is a real thing. Pairs sitting along the embankment appear to maintain near-identical distances between them — roughly 1.8 meters. It's been measured. Whether it's cultural, spatial, or coincidence has never been fully settled. Kyoto people treat it as obvious. Visitors from elsewhere stop and count.

facts.kid: A Japanese coffee chain (Komeda's) with a Pokemon-themed promotion! You had the Kuro-neige baumkuchen dessert.
facts.tip: Apr 25 5:41 PM, Kyoto.
facts.wow: Komeda's Coffee was founded in Nagoya in 1968 and is now Japan's #1 indie chain (vs. Starbucks #1 foreign chain).
facts.local: Their signature: free 'morning service' - order coffee 7-11 AM and get free toast + boiled egg.

extra_cards.title: Booked the hotel right here
extra_cards.body: 5 PM. Over Pokemon chocolate dessert at Komeda. No hotel in Kyoto, no plan, one night left. Pulled up the Marriott app. Four Points Flex by Sheraton Kyoto Oike — available, walkable to Gion, priced right. Booked it. Done. The whole decision took about three minutes.

pins.title: Four Points Flex by Sheraton Kyoto Oike

facts.kid: Bryan's Kyoto base — booked same-day, no plan, walked there from across the city after a 2-hour detour along the river.
facts.tip: Breakfast photos exist. Marriott Bonvoy member — standard booking, easy choice, no mental energy spent.
facts.wow: Japanese Marriott properties sometimes provide yukata robes in rooms — a nod to traditional inn culture in a modern hotel.
facts.local: The front desk staff are sharp. Bryan asked how to walk to the shrines. She said take the subway. He said he preferred to walk. She said it was too far. He showed her where he'd walked the day before. She was shocked, said 'how many hours did it take?' — and then told him how to walk.

extra_cards.title: No hotel. No plan.
extra_cards.body:
Bryan left Tokyo for Kyoto with no hotel booked. People thought he was crazy. Kel asked how he could travel to a city for a weekend with no idea where he was sleeping.

His thinking: he didn't know what he'd be doing or where he'd end up. Spending energy on a hotel decision felt like wasted mental space — he's not great at picking hotels and doesn't care that much. He's a Marriott member. It would sort itself out.

It was about 5 PM when he decided he should figure out where to sleep. He was at a coffee shop, had been wandering Kyoto's shrines and alleys since morning. He booked the Four Points Flex by Sheraton Kyoto Oike. Easy. Done. Back to wandering.

extra_cards.title: The river detour
extra_cards.body:
The hotel was a long walk from where he was. He figured he'd walk anyway — he'd been doing that all trip. He took videos for Kel along the way. Called her at some point.

Then he saw a big river.

He was already hours into walking. The hotel was close-ish. But a river.

He detoured. Down random alleys, ended up on the riverbank walk. Couples sitting together at the edge. Calm. Quiet. The lights starting to come up as the sun went down. It reminded him of Amsterdam — beautiful in the same way.

He sat for a while. Rested. Took it in. Missed Kel.

Eventually he decided he was actually tired and pointed himself at the hotel.

extra_cards.title: The front desk lady
extra_cards.body:
Every morning Bryan would talk to the front desk. Same routine: tell them his game plan, get feedback, ask for anything cool to see or do. Then point himself in a direction and go.

The morning he left Kyoto, he told the front desk lady he wanted to walk all day and see shrines. She recommended the subway. He said he preferred to walk. She said it was too far. They went back and forth.

He pointed to the map — showed her the shrines he'd been to the day before. Told her he'd walked from there to the hotel yesterday.

She stared at him. 'How many hours did it take?'

He told her he had no idea. He didn't mention the river detour. Figured that would be too much to process.

She said 'ok ok' and told him how to walk there. He thanked her and started walking.

facts.kid: Kyoto chocolate shop in a European-style building with a big clock.
facts.wow: Japanese craft chocolate has won 100+ International Chocolate Awards in the last decade - punching well above its size.
facts.local: Bean-to-bar shops cluster around Pontocho/Kiyamachi. Walking the river bank you'll pass 3 in 4 blocks.
The shrine at the bottom of the main slope (Bishamonten Zenkokuji) is where Kagurazaka geisha have prayed for centuries.
facts.history: JNI deep-dive meeting day in Kagurazaka — formal Visitor Temporary Pass at Ichigaya, then JNI office.
facts.wow: Kagurazaka is a historic geisha district; today it's a quietly upscale neighborhood with French expats and traditional restaurants on cobblestone streets.
facts.tip: Apr 21 morning. Lexus dashboard commute, External Visitor Temporary Pass photo.

extra_cards.title: Couldn't find the office
extra_cards.body: Everyone was spiffy. Decks finalized, translations done, pitches locked. The whole team was pumped. Then the Uber dropped them off and that was about the last thing that went smoothly. Wrong address. They walked up and down and around streets, calling the contact. The partner had recently moved to shared office space and the address hadn't been updated. Arrived late, tired, and already sweaty. Then jumped straight into it.

extra_cards.title: The American brings peanut butter cups
extra_cards.body: They brought gifts — the team brought Dutch items, Bryan contributed peanut butter cups as the American. Big hit. The meeting itself was very strong. Better connection than expected, more leads generated, training delivered. The need is clearly there, the solution fits, the timing is right. They left with a solid pipeline result and real momentum.

extra_cards.title: Puffer fish — round one
extra_cards.body: Traditional Japanese lunch near the partner's shared space in the middle of the day. Bryan had puffer fish (fugu) for the first time. He lived. Verdict: 'It was only ok tasting. Not risking your life good.'

facts.local: The Tokyo Bay business district (Toyosu / Shibaura) is where most Japanese conglomerate headquarters relocated when central Tokyo got too expensive.
facts.history: Bryan's 'never thought I'd conduct business in a Tokyo highrise' day. Full NSSOL deep-dive.
facts.wow: Nippon Steel Solutions (NSSOL) is the IT arm of Nippon Steel — they run major systems for Japanese banking, government, and steel manufacturing.
facts.tip: Apr 23. Dark suit hotel mirror selfie at 7:50 AM, NSSOL deep-dive ran 10:00 AM – 3:30 PM.

extra_cards.title: The shoes
extra_cards.body: Bryan bought a new pair of Oxford classic dress shoes specifically for this trip. Wore them around the house for days before leaving — intentional break-in, not fashion. He knew what Tokyo's streets would do to unbroken leather. The morning of the NSSOL meeting: fresh suit, new shoes, briefcase. He was locked in. The kind of focused that makes you feel like you could walk through a brick wall.

extra_cards.title: The highrise moment
extra_cards.body: Walking into the Tokyo Bay business district that morning stopped him for a second. Glass and steel towers, high-security lobby, business people moving with purpose. He had a beat of stepping outside himself: I am here. Never in a million years did he think he'd be conducting business in a Tokyo highrise. Full team in the elevator — everyone standing in perfect orderly silence. Clair started giggling.

extra_cards.title: The day they wildly exceeded
extra_cards.body: Full deep-dive with their biggest partner. Three goals on the agenda: walk through materials for the client sessions ahead, train them on the platform, explore new business development. Bryan went in with a personal pipeline target. They blew past it — multiple new leads, meetings set up for that same week, the partner team immediately energized by the new solutions. Great traditional Japanese lunch mid-day. No sitting on the floor, which was a relief. New team members connected with naturally. The day ran exactly how you hope a business trip can run.

facts.kid: Tokyo's famous immersive digital-art museum. Pitch-dark rooms where light, lasers, and mirrors create infinite illusions you can walk through. The team-building outing.
facts.tip: The icicle-room Bryan remembers is 'Crystal Universe' — hanging strands of LEDs reflected in mirrored walls and floor, looks infinite in every direction.
facts.wow: teamLab Borderless reopened in February 2024 at Azabudai Hills (a new Mori Building complex with shopping + offices + residences). The famous original location in Odaiba closed in 2022; this is the revived version with new installations.
facts.local: Tickets sell out — you book a time slot in advance. Plan ~2 hours inside. Wear comfortable shoes; the floors mirror, so socks-only in some rooms.

extra_cards.title: The team outing
extra_cards.body: Wednesday's team-building. After the first MoD meeting, the crew walked to a part of Tokyo Bryan had never seen — less fancy than Ginza, more corporate, big-city. The place turned out to be a futuristic museum: room after room, each one a different immersive world across every wall.

extra_cards.title: The rooms Bryan remembers
extra_cards.body:
The water-floor room — the lines on the floor followed you like you were walking on water.

The sunflower room — 3D sunflowers moving across every surface, overwhelming. Bryan thought of Kel, who loves sunflowers and is smothering in the good and annoying ways. He felt smothered by sunflowers. He missed her.

The wave room — a small room with a bench, walls of strong, active water. 'I sat in that room for a while to get washed.'

The icicle room — Crystal Universe: hanging LED strands mirrored into infinity.

extra_cards.title: Hurry up sweetheart and take that pic
extra_cards.body: Selfies everywhere. Bryan got it — it's a cool place. But after a while: places to be. Older-brother energy, the whole trip.

facts.local: Locals always pick HND over NRT when they can — HND is 30 minutes from central Tokyo by train, NRT is 90+.
facts.history: Return flight: UA804 HND -> IAD, 15:45 departure. Bryan's last hours in Japan.
facts.wow: Haneda was the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic for most of the 1980s — overtaken only when Narita opened the second Tokyo gateway.
facts.tip: Apr 27. HND ramen for lunch before boarding.

facts.kid: Bryan walked the empty streets near his hotel at 5:41 AM and caught Tsukiji Hongan-ji Temple's stone dome in the early morning light.
facts.wow: Tsukiji Hongan-ji (築地本願寺, built 1934) is designed by architect Ito Chuta in an ancient Indian style — stone columns, a dome, and lotus-cap ornament that look nothing like a typical Japanese temple. Ito argued Buddhism's origins traced back through China to South Asia, so the temple should look the part.
facts.local: At 5 AM the market vendors are deep in work. The commercial streets are empty. The red lights change for no cars.
facts.tip: Bryan walked this route several mornings. By end of trip it felt like his street.

extra_cards.title: Tokyo at 5:41 AM
extra_cards.body:
The city was empty. Not Tsukiji-market empty — the outer market had been awake since 3 AM. This was the commercial streets empty. Red light, no cars. A motorbike crosses the wide intersection. The early sky is that particular Tokyo morning color: pale gold and grey.

The temple dome to the right — stone, domed, unmistakably not Japanese at first glance. He'd passed it a half-dozen times before he looked up the name.

By the last day, this crossing felt like his.

facts.kid: The famous tree-lined boulevard between Tokyo Station and Yurakucho — zelkova trees, Japan Post red mailboxes, and glass towers on both sides.
facts.wow: Marunouchi (丸の内, 'inside the circle') was the outer ring of the original Edo Castle moat. Today it holds the densest concentration of corporate headquarters in Japan.
facts.local: In winter the zelkova trees are lit up for the Marunouchi Illumination — 3M+ visitors, Nov–Feb. In April they're just leafing out green.
facts.tip: Bryan walked south from Tokyo Station at 17:32 on Day 9 — his last evening walk in Tokyo before flying home.

facts.kid: The lively commercial zone just south of Tokyo Station — pawn shops, gaming arcades, and one of Tokyo's hidden peace monuments.
facts.wow: The Peace Bell monument on Yaesu Avenue has 26 bells imported from the Netherlands — built in 1989 to mark Chuo Ward's Peace City Declaration. It rings on the hour.
facts.local: Under the elevated JR tracks around Yurakucho station sit some of the best cheap yakitori in Tokyo — izakayas that have operated since the 1940s, unchanged.
facts.tip: Bryan photographed the 高価買取 (high-value buyback) pawn shop at 17:35 — and the Peace Bell at 17:42.

extra_cards.title: The Dutch bells
extra_cards.body:
Yaesu Avenue median — 7 meters tall, 26 bells from the Netherlands. Installed 1989. First anniversary of Chuo Ward's Peace City Declaration.

Bryan walked past it alone on his last evening, returning from Kyoto. He'd spent the week with Doug — his Dutch colleague — walking Tokyo streets together. The bells were Dutch. The week had been Dutch.

The Netherlands kept showing up on this trip.

facts.kid: The most famous luxury shopping district in Japan — at dusk, with the stores lit up and the backstreets busy.
facts.wow: Ginza land values are the highest in Japan — over ¥32M per square meter at the 4-chome crossing. A parking space in Ginza can cost more than a house in rural Japan.
facts.local: On weekends, Ginza's main avenues go car-free (歩行者天国 — 'Pedestrian Paradise'). Weekday evening, cars are back and the pace is different — more purposeful, less tourist.
facts.tip: 17:57–18:04 on Day 9. Hotel was close. Last walk of the last full day.

facts.kid: A metal sculpture outside the Tsukiji Zodiac Building (Eto Building) — whale-fin shapes rising from a granite base with a compass rose inlaid in the pavement below.
facts.wow: Tsukiji means 'land built on the sea' (築地) — the entire neighborhood is Edo-period reclaimed land, dredged from Tokyo Bay.
facts.local: The Eto (干支) refers to the Japanese zodiac cycle — the 12 animals that name years. The building's public art program weaves all 12 through its design.
facts.tip: Bryan photographed this at 18:11 on Day 9 — the last photo of his last evening walk. The hotel was two blocks away.

extra_cards.title: The walk ends here
extra_cards.body:
Day 9. Bryan had flown back from Kyoto that morning, dropped his bag at the hotel, and walked out the door again. Tokyo Station to Marunouchi, south through Yurakucho, into Ginza, then all the way back to the hotel neighborhood.

He found the carillon by walking past it. The compass rose in the pavement. The metal whale-fins of the sculpture. He stopped and took the photo.

18:11 PM. The hotel was two blocks away. Dinner somewhere close. Last night in Japan.

facts.kid: The big domed temple near Bryan's hotel — he walked past it nearly every day. It looks like an ancient Indian temple, not a Japanese one.
facts.tip: About a 3-minute walk from the Mitsui Garden Hotel Ginza Tsukiji. Photographed at dawn and again across the trip.
facts.wow: The whole neighborhood is named after this temple. 築地 'Tsukiji' literally means 'reclaimed land' — after the temple burned in the Great Fire of 1657, its followers reclaimed wetland from the river by hand to rebuild it. The famous fish market came centuries later.
facts.local: Jodo Shinshu (True Pure Land) Buddhism, a branch of Kyoto's Nishi Honganji. Stained glass, carved animals, and a pipe organ inside — almost unheard-of in a Buddhist temple. Not a 'fortune' temple; that's Senso-ji.

extra_cards.title: Hidden in plain sight
extra_cards.body:
Bryan walked past it a hundred times — the great domed temple a few minutes from the hotel — and only later learned it was the origin point of the entire neighborhood.

Founded in 1617. Burned in the Great Fire of 1657. There was no land to rebuild on, so its followers reclaimed wetland from the Sumida River by hand. That reclaimed ground is what 'Tsukiji' means. Burned again after the 1923 earthquake. Rebuilt, in 1934, in the ancient-Indian style it wears now.

A temple that burned down twice and was rebuilt twice — the second time on ground that had to be made before it could be built on. Things that survive.

facts.kid: A small Kyoto temple where Bryan found the Bussokuseki — the Buddha's Footprints, carved into stone, larger than life.
facts.tip: Day 9 morning, on the walk from the Marriott toward the Kyoto Round Trail. This was the FIRST footprints stone Bryan found — around 10:02 — and the one where he prayed. He photographed others as he came across them through the day.
facts.wow: Bussokuseki — 'Buddha's Footprints stones' — are among the oldest objects of Buddhist veneration, older than Buddha statues. They mark where the Buddha is said to have stood.
facts.local: Found by wandering — a quiet neighborhood temple, not a tour-bus stop. The kind of place you only reach on foot.

extra_cards.title: The first footprints stone
extra_cards.body: The first one Bryan found. He'd photograph others as he came across them through the day, but this was the first — a Bussokuseki, the Buddha's footprints carved into stone, larger than life. He stepped onto it, lined his feet up with the carved prints, and stared down with all his questions and no answers. Then he prayed for God to guide his path — today and forever. That's how he started the day's journey.

extra_cards.title: Guided steps
extra_cards.body:
People pray for their steps and actions to be guided. Does that mean predetermined? Is it a push or a pull? Something you realize you're in at the time, or only later? How do you align yourself with the guided path — and what's required of you to move along it?

Bryan's honest answer: no idea. He just knows that when he looks back on his life — the moments he let go of control and followed the path — he usually finds ways to be useful to other people, and picks up some good stories along the way. Enjoying his steps as they lead him to serve. That's the goal. He just needs to know where to go.

'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.' Humility is always the first step. His prayer at this stone, and at every temple after it, started the same way: humbly admitting he doesn't know, asking for guidance — and then start moving.

facts.kid: Bryan's favorite souvenir: a purple silk book filled with hand-brushed shrine stamps, plus a navy military stamp book, plus charms and fortunes tucked between the pages.
facts.tip: Two books came home. Book 1: the purple goshuin book — Meiji Jingu, Zojo-ji, Fushimi Inari, and Himukai Daijingu. Book 2: a navy 'Kichi-in-cho' base-stamp book with the Ministry of Defense visit stamp.
facts.wow: A goshuin (御朱印, 'honorable red seal') is proof of pilgrimage — the site name in brush calligraphy, a red seal, and the date. Each one is unique because it is hand-calligraphed the specific day you were there.
facts.local: Some shrines hand-write the goshuin live; high-traffic ones issue pre-printed slips. Bryan's book holds both, plus pamphlets, omamori envelopes, and talisman cards — a scrapbook as much as a stamp book.

extra_cards.title: A witness, not a souvenir
extra_cards.body: Each goshuin is hand-calligraphed the specific day you stand there — the site name in brush ink, the red seal, the date. It isn't bought; it's received, at the shrine office, after you've visited. Bryan's purple book holds Meiji Jingu, Zojo-ji's bold single-character 本堂 ('Main Hall') drawn by a priest, Fushimi Inari, and Himukai Daijingu — the Kyoto cave shrine that became his favorite of the trip. Less a stamp collection than a record of where he stood.

extra_cards.title: THE LEAST FORTUNATE
extra_cards.body:
Senso-ji omikuji #31. The official tier is 末小吉 — 'ending small fortune' — and the English on the slip reads 'FINAL, THE LEAST FORTUNATE.'

The poem underneath is the kun-fish from Zhuangzi: the giant fish that has not yet transformed into the great bird. 'A chance doesn't come yet... stand still on the shoreline, waiting.' Then the wind and clouds rise, and the fish crosses the heavens.

Bryan kept it. The lowest fortune in Japan, and obviously the best one he could have drawn — latent potential, waiting for its catalyst, in a year he was rebuilding himself.

extra_cards.title: From the empress
extra_cards.body:
At Meiji Jingu, Bryan drew a second fortune 'from the empress.' He meant it literally. Meiji Jingu doesn't grade its fortunes — it gives you a waka poem written by Emperor Meiji or Empress Shoken herself.

Poem #22, by Empress Shoken:

'Every morning / We gaze into our mirrors / Which are unblemished; / Oh, that we could attain / Such a purity of soul.'

Tucked in the same sleeve: an ink drawing of a leaping hare and a fox — lifted straight from the Choju-giga, the 12th-century scrolls considered the oldest manga in Japan.

extra_cards.title: The victory-luck eagle
extra_cards.body:
From Zojo-ji, the Tokugawa family temple: a talisman card with a white-headed hawk and two characters — 勝運 (victory luck) and 成就 (fulfillment). First you win, then you finish.

The hawk is no accident. Tokugawa Ieyasu was a lifelong falconer; the card is a line straight to the Kuro-honzon, the blackened Amida Buddha he carried into every battle. The card itself is printed: 'A GOOD-LUCK CHARM · Zojoji temple, since 1393 · TOKYO JAPAN.'
